b: A guaranteed campaign is an advertising purchase in which the seller promises, before anything runs, to deliver an agreed quantity of ads at an agreed price over an agreed period. The quantity is usually a number of impressions, a share of a placement or, in television, a ratings target. The publisher sets that inventory aside so no other buyer can take it, and if delivery falls short the publisher owes a remedy. It exists because advertisers planning a launch or a seasonal push need certainty about reach and cost, and publishers want committed revenue before the month begins.

The opposite is the non-guaranteed buy: an auction campaign in which the advertiser bids for impressions as they appear and pays only for what it wins. Guaranteed campaigns remain the core of premium publishing, connected television (CTV) and the television upfront market.
How a guaranteed campaign is built

A buyer and a publisher's sales team first agree terms in an insertion order, or IO, specifying the placements, targeting, flight dates, volume and price. Price is most often expressed as CPM, cost per thousand impressions, though sponsorships can be sold at a flat rate per day.

The publisher then checks whether it can honour the order. Ad servers forecast inventory by matching the requested targeting against historical traffic and campaigns already booked. Google Ad Manager flags line items that are "Expected to underdeliver" if they start within 30 days, end within a year and carry an absolute goal. When the forecast clears, the inventory is reserved.

Inside the ad server, the order becomes one or more line items, the records that tell the system what to serve, where and how often. Google's documentation is direct about the mapping: "If you want to offer guaranteed inventory to an advertiser or buyer, use Sponsorship or Standard line items."
Sponsorship line items run at priority 4 and serve "based upon a defined percentage of impressions and a start and end time". A one-day homepage takeover is the classic case.
Standard line items run at priority 6, 8 or 10 and serve against "a defined impression goal".
Non-guaranteed types - Network, Bulk, Price Priority, Ad Exchange and AdSense - sit at priority 12, with House ads at 16.

Lower numbers win. Google states that guaranteed line items occupy "the priority range of 1 to 10", and that priority 11 "is no longer available for new reservation line items". Since May 1, 2020, Ad Manager has restricted each line item type to a defined purpose.

Other ad servers use different numbers for the same idea. Microsoft Monetize, formerly Xandr, calls its version a guaranteed delivery augmented line item. Impression-goal line items there "typically" run at priorities 11 to 17, with a default of 14, while exclusive share-of-voice line items run at 18 to 20, defaulting to 19. Booking defaults to "Save and Reserve", which holds inventory "so the impressions cannot be allocated to other line items", according to Microsoft's documentation, updated September 1, 2026.

Once live, the ad server spreads delivery across the flight. Ad Manager's default, Evenly, can deliver up to 5% above goal as a safeguard. Monetize defaults to a daily pace of 105% of even delivery. A campaign that falls behind schedule is given more competitive weight. Google says a lagging guaranteed line item "wins often enough to stay on pace".

A worked example shows the economics. A publisher books 2 million impressions at a $25 CPM over 30 days, a $50,000 order. If traffic dips and the campaign ends at 1.8 million, the publisher is 10% short and owes the buyer either 200,000 extra impressions in a later makegood flight or a credit of $5,000. The usual causes of such gaps are set out in PPC Land's under-delivery explainer.

Guaranteed does not mean exclusive access to every impression a campaign could use. Ad Manager's dynamic allocation assigns each Standard line item a temporary CPM for each impression, based on its delivery progress, and lets exchange demand take the impression if it pays more than "the opportunity cost of not serving" the guaranteed campaign. The direct buyer still receives its contracted volume, though not necessarily the same impressions, a point now central to litigation.

Guaranteed buying predates digital media. Television networks have long sold audience guarantees in the annual upfront market, promising a ratings level for a package of spots and compensating shortfalls with free inventory known as audience deficiency units (ADUs).

Online, the first common contract rules came on March 19, 2001, when the American Association of Advertising Agencies (4A's) and the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB) jointly issued Terms and Conditions for Internet Advertising. Among other rules, "the first 30 days of a campaign are firm", according to the IAB announcement. Version 3.0, published in 2010, added specifics in Section VI: the publisher must warn the agency of likely under-delivery no later than 14 days before the IO ends, then negotiate a makegood or allow a credit. The same section draws the boundary of the concept: for cost-per-click, cost-per-lead and cost-per-acquisition deliverables, "guaranteed delivery, even delivery, and makegoods are not available."

Automation followed. In September 2013 the IAB's "Programmatic and Automation" paper defined automated guaranteed as a sale in which "the inventory and pricing are guaranteed, and the campaign runs at the same priority as other direct deals in the ad server". It listed rival market names including programmatic guaranteed and programmatic premium. Google opened a public beta of programmatic guaranteed deals on January 12, 2016 and made them generally available on April 5, 2017. Display & Video 360 (DV360), Google's demand-side platform, extended programmatic guaranteed support to FreeWheel, Kargo, Smartclip and Xandr in September 2020, and Google extended percentage-based sponsorship goals to programmatic guaranteed deals in March 2022, as PPC Land's share of voice explainer records.

For publishers, guaranteed campaigns are usually the highest-priced inventory and the most predictable revenue. They also depend on a sales force. Grindr's chief executive George Arison said in August 2026 that the company still faced "significant challenges in getting advertisers to work directly with Grindr", even as its advertising revenue rose 44% to $25 million.

For buyers, the premium paid transfers forecasting risk to the seller, a trade common in CTV. Amazon introduced guaranteed deals for Prime Video ads on August 1, 2024. Its DSP documentation now states that "Guaranteed ad groups can only target a single PG or PG-SOV deal" - PG-SOV being programmatic guaranteed share of voice - as noted in coverage of Amazon's streaming TV budget calculator on November 17, 2026.
Retail media has adopted the model too. Amazon introduced reserve share of voice for branded search in October 2025, selling Sponsored Brands top-of-search placements at a fixed upfront price.

The first weakness is measurement. When the publisher's ad server and the buyer's verification vendor count differently, both can claim compliance. The IAB's 2026 draft contract framework, open for comment from February 12 to March 31, 2026, proposed treating a discrepancy above 10% as under-delivery if reconciliation fails, along with a two-business-day notice and a ten-business-day remedy window, as described in PPC Land's coverage of the framework.

The second is that makegoods are an imperfect cure. Free impressions in January do not replace a missed holiday weekend. Streaming showed the problem in December 2022, when Netflix let advertisers recover money after delivering in some cases "roughly 80% of the expected audience", according to Digiday, which cited agency executives.

The third is the strength of the word itself. Amazon's reserve share of voice promises top-of-search placement "most of the time". "They are not guaranteeing 100% impression share," Alexander Swade, an Amazon advertising specialist, said in PPC Land's coverage of the launch.

The fourth concerns who decides which impressions a guaranteed buyer receives. On September 30, 2026, Judge P. Kevin Castel in New York refused to end the Gannett and Daily Mail suits against Google, finding that "a reasonable jury could find" that enhanced dynamic allocation, introduced in 2014 to let exchange bids compete with guaranteed line items, caused antitrust injury. The publishers' economist Ali Hortacsu put the reduction in the global value of direct sales at approximately 24.1%, as reported when Castel sent the damages claims to a jury. Google disputes the claims; no finding has been made.
Programmatic guaranteed. A guaranteed campaign executed through a DSP with a deal ID instead of manual trafficking; a subset, not a different promise.
Preferred deal. A fixed price and first look at inventory, with no reservation and no volume commitment from either side.
Sponsorship. A guaranteed campaign sold as a percentage of impressions on a placement or section, rather than a fixed impression count.
Direct-sold campaign. Any campaign sold by a publisher's own team. Many are guaranteed, but direct sales can also be non-guaranteed, as PPC Land's direct sales channel explainer shows.

Guaranteed inventory is now a battleground in automated buying. On August 6, 2026, The Trade Desk's chief executive Jeff Green said some competitors "have been focused on producing products for Programmatic Guaranteed, fixed price transactions" and that "some are even wrapping these in agentic technologies", PPC Land reported in its piece on rivals wrapping guaranteed deals in agentic AI at 1% fees. IAB Tech Lab added programmatic guaranteed to version 2.0 of its Agentic Advertising Management Protocols (AAMP) in April 2026.

The legal frame around the ad server is also shifting. On September 2, 2026, Judge Leonie Brinkema in Virginia declined to order a sale of Google's ad exchange and imposed conduct rules instead, while the Gannett and Daily Mail claims over how guaranteed impressions were allocated head toward a jury. How a delivery promise is fulfilled, not only whether it is, is now a matter for the courts.

Who. Publishers' direct sales and ad operations teams sell and traffic guaranteed campaigns; advertisers and agencies buy them through insertion orders or, increasingly, through DSPs such as DV360, Amazon DSP and The Trade Desk. Ad server operators, chiefly Google Ad Manager and Microsoft Monetize, run the reservation and pacing systems. The IAB and the 4A's write the standard contract terms.

What. A purchase in which the seller reserves inventory and commits in advance to a fixed volume, share or audience at a fixed price, owing a makegood or credit if delivery falls short. In Ad Manager it runs as Sponsorship or Standard line items at priorities 1 to 10, ahead of all auction demand.

When. Rooted in television's upfront guarantees, it was codified online by the first IAB/4A's terms on March 19, 2001, automated by programmatic guaranteed products from 2016, and extended into retail media and CTV through 2024 to 2026.

Where. In the publisher ad server, at the top of the line item priority stack, and in contracts negotiated between sellers and buyers, across display, video, CTV, television and retail media placements.

Why. Advertisers pay for certainty of reach and timing, and publishers gain committed, higher-priced revenue. The model is contested over how delivery is measured, whether makegoods compensate missed moments, how firm "guaranteed" really is, and whether ad server owners allocated guaranteed impressions fairly.
